header: Date/Time: 2025-11-20 15:00 UTC | Duration: 52m | Location: Zoom | Recording: yes | Link: https://redwood.app/meet/HE-1120
summary: Weekly POC sync focused on reducing Time-To-First-Token (TTFT) and improving streaming stability across long sequences. Reviewed last week's bench: first-byte wins with kernel A on short sequences but regresses for 8k+ tokens; KV cache warm-up variability noted. Action items: run 10k request stress, share kernel matrix, customer to provide sequence distribution and schedule kernel toggle benchmark next week.
topics: TTFT baseline review, streaming fragmentation and chunk size, sequence-length effects, kernel selection tradeoffs, caching strategy (KV cache), quantization impacts, next steps for benchmarking and pricing/pilot terms
transcript:
00:00 Maya: Alright everyone, thanks for joining. We have about 50 minutes, agenda is TTFT and kernel path review, quick bench recap, and next steps. Samir's going to walk through the numbers.
00:08 Samir: Hey team, thanks. So quick context — last week we ran the pilot runs on three kernel families, labeled A, B, C. Short answer: A is fastest for 128-512 token sequences for first byte, B is most consistent at 2k, and C shows benefits with 8k but has higher variance. Some notes — the streaming fragmentation we saw earlier seems tied to chunking and the client-side buffering.
00:30 Markus: When you say "first byte" are we talking average or p50/p99? We care about p99 cold-starts for interactive features.
00:35 Samir: Good call. We collected p50/p90/p99. For TTFT cold (no KV cache): A p50 = 160ms, p99 = 420ms; B p50 = 190ms, p99 = 360ms; C p50 = 225ms, p99 = 500ms — but for longer sequences (4k+) B's p99 stays near 480ms while A spikes.
00:58 Lena: Sorry can I clarify — when you say cold, is that new process or cold cache? Our workload reuses contexts a lot for the same session.
01:03 Samir: It's cold KV cache and cold model worker — we have separate warm runs. Warm-cache p99s were much lower: A warm p99=210ms, B warm p99=200ms. So KV cache warm-up helps A a lot. There's also a variance if there are lots of in-flight requests — batching policy interacts.
01:22 Priya: Right, our traffic has bursty spikes, so that initial window is critical. How much of this is infra vs kernel choice?
01:28 Samir: Both. Kernel A uses a fused attention kernel that benefits short sequences — that's mostly model-level. B uses an alternative matmul schedule with lower tail variance. But infra config — thread pinning, NUMA placement, GPU MIG/SM allocation — matters for p99 as well.
01:40 Markus: Any quantization differences? We're on q4_0 in our pilot.
01:44 Samir: We ran q4 and int8-ish profiles. Quantization changed throughput but didn't materially change TTFT unless it affected kernel selection — some kernels are more quant-friendly. C leveraged a custom kernel that isn't fully quantized optimized, so C's long-seq perf benefits came at some quantization cost.
02:02 Maya: Quick interjection — on the streaming side we saw customers hit jitter where the UI waits then dumps a large chunk. Is that the fragmentation you mentioned?
02:10 Samir: Yeah, fragmentation is two-fold: server chunking (how the model slices outputs for streaming) and client buffer thresholds. Our default chunk is 512 tokens or 200ms; with long responses that yields irregular updates.
02:24 Lena: We can tweak the client but we'd prefer server-side smoothing so front-end code doesn't need a ton of logic.
02:29 Samir: Agreed — we can change the chunk policy; switching to smaller chunks with a max latency floor helped in our internal tests but increased request overhead, so it's a cost tradeoff.
02:41 Markus: For our success criteria we defined: p99 TTFT < 300ms for interactive flows and streaming latency under 350ms for incremental updates. Can you hit that?
02:50 Samir: Depends on sequence distribution. For short 256-ish sequences, yes with kernel A and warm cache. For 2k+ sequences we need kernel B and some infra tuning — we can approach it but might need a dedicated pool to guarantee p99 SLAs.
03:05 Priya: So dedicated vs hosted again — our security team wants VPC and customer-managed keys. That pushes us to Redwood Private. Does kernel behavior change in private?
03:14 Maya: The runtime is the same, but the infra knobs you'll control (VM configs, kernel modules) give you more deterministic NUMA and GPU allocation. We typically see +/-10-15% tail improvements with a tuned private deployment.
03:26 Lena: You mentioned fallback models earlier. Is that automatic?
03:29 Samir: We have routing policies — on overload we can fallback to a smaller compatible model variant to preserve p99 latency. But that affects quality. We can orchestrate canary/fallback thresholds.
03:38 Markus: Did you test with our real prompts? We sent a sample set last week — were those in the bench?
03:42 Samir: Yes, we ingested the sample file (names had a couple transcribe hiccups, "Helix---health prompts" got parsed odd) but we ran them through kernels A/B/C. Results are in the benchmark spreadsheet: https://redwood.app/b/helix-bench-1120 — note column headers have some manual cleanup.
03:59 Lena: On KV cache, what's warmup cost? We saw a spike on first session of like 800ms.
04:06 Samir: That 800ms matches cold model + cold KV. Our suggestion: pre-warm on session start asynchronously or keep a pool of warmed workers. Prefetching embeddings also helps. We can demo a warm-pool config.
04:22 Maya: Actionable ask — Priya, can you share your 48h sequence-length distribution? That will determine default kernel choice.
04:29 Priya: Yes I can. I can either share histograms or a small sample. We'll aim for histogram by Friday.
04:34 Markus: Also please include concurrency patterns — number of concurrent sessions typical.
04:37 Priya: Will add that.
04:40 Samir: Another point — for kernel toggles we can do an A/B bench on identical hardware: spin two pools, toggle routing, and measure p99/TTFT/throughput for the same prompt set. That should isolate kernel effects from infra.
04:54 Maya: How long do those runs usually take?
04:56 Samir: For statistical significance we recommend at least 10k requests over varied concurrency windows — about 4-6 hours depending on burst pattern. For a quick sanity bench 1k requests over controlled concurrency is ~30 minutes.
05:07 Lena: Ok let's do a short sanity run first, then the 10k. Priya, does next Tuesday work for the longer run?
05:13 Priya: Tuesday afternoon is good.
05:15 Samir: I'll prepare the kernel-selection matrix and a doc that lists caveats: memory usage, quant-compat, fallback compatibility.
05:23 Maya: Pricing — we agreed to share pilot commit options based on dedicated pool sizing and expected token volume. I'll send two options: 50% reserved pool and 100% reserved pool with fallback.
05:33 Markus: We'll need an estimate of cost delta when you switch to smaller chunk sizes for streaming since that increases token overhead.
05:39 Maya: We'll quantify that — Samir, can you estimate delta for chunk sizes 512 vs 256 vs 128?
05:44 Samir: Yes, rough numbers in the doc, I'll update with bench results after the runs. 256 tends to increase request count by ~7-10% depending on typical response length; 128 is higher overhead but better UI responsiveness.
05:58 Lena: One more security question — audit log granularity for streaming events and per-token tracing. We need to satisfy audit requirements.
06:04 Maya: Redwood can provide per-request logs, and we can redact tokens at rest if needed. For Private we can integrate with your KMS/HSM. We'll share the security pack: https://redwood.app/docs/helix-security
06:14 Markus: Good. Any blockers left?
06:17 Priya: Need to see the kernel A/B matrix and sequence histograms. Also need the runner to schedule the 10k bench with us.
06:23 Samir: We'll schedule and bring the infra hooks; I'll also include a runbook for reproducing results.
06:28 Maya: Great. Recap: Redwood runs quick sanity bench and longer 10k run next Tuesday (Samir). Helix shares sequence and concurrency histograms (Priya). Maya sends pricing/pilot choices and benchmark link. Samir shares kernel matrix by Monday.
06:43 Lena: Sounds good. Thanks everyone.
06:46 Maya: Thanks, we'll follow up in email with calendar invite and artifacts.
06:50 System: Link to bench: https://redwood.app/b/helix-bench-1120; security pack: https://redwood.app/docs/helix-security
06:55 End of recording.
